<reason>A more convincingly evaluated the proposition as accepting increased risk, not guaranteeing recession. It directly explained what prioritization requires and connected restraint to rent-setting power and the cumulative costs of delay. B’s construction and income objections remained substantial, but its repeated movement from inelastic demand to ineffective restraint, and from recession risk to inevitable lost paychecks, weakened its comparison. A handled the central pressure more honestly and consistently.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A challenged B’s claim that tightening “guarantees” entrenched shortages and its comparison of another year’s rent increases with certain job loss. B supplied credible harm mechanisms but did not adequately repair those overstatements. A then explicitly accepted employment risk rather than evading what its proposed priority entails.</best_rebuttal>
